subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What defines a ferrous metal?
options: It contains no iron at all
questions.explain: Ferrous metals contain iron, which is why most are magnetic and prone to rusting.

questions.q: Hardwoods are obtained from which type of tree?
questions.explain: Hardwoods come from deciduous, broadleaf trees such as oak and mahogany, which are generally slow-growing.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a thermosetting polymer?
options: It can be reheated and reshaped many times
It cannot be reheated and reshaped once set
It softens whenever it is warmed
questions.explain: Thermosetting polymers undergo a permanent chemical change when set and cannot be softened and reshaped by reheating.

questions.q: What does the physical property 'density' describe?
options: The mass per unit volume of a material
The resistance of a material to scratching
The ability of a material to conduct heat
The ability of a material to return to shape
questions.explain: Density is a physical property defined as mass per unit volume, affecting how heavy a product feels.

questions.q: A material described as malleable can best be:
options: Hammered or rolled into sheets without cracking
Stretched and then return to shape
Melted at a very low temperature
questions.explain: Malleability is the ability to be deformed by compression, such as hammering or rolling into sheets, without cracking.

questions.q: Which property describes a material's ability to absorb impact or shock without fracturing?
questions.explain: Toughness is the ability to absorb impact energy and resist sudden shock loads without breaking.

questions.q: Brass is an alloy made mainly from which two metals?
questions.explain: Brass is a non-ferrous alloy of copper and zinc, valued for its corrosion resistance and appearance.

questions.q: MDF (medium-density fibreboard) is an example of which material category?
questions.explain: MDF is a manufactured board made by bonding wood fibres with resin under heat and pressure.

questions.q: A jeweller needs a metal that can be drawn out into fine wire without breaking. Which property is essential?
questions.explain: Ductility is the ability to be drawn out into wires under tension without fracturing.

questions.q: In material selection, which factor relates to the visual appeal, colour and texture of a material?
questions.explain: Aesthetics concerns how a material looks and feels, including its colour, texture and finish.

questions.q: A wood chisel blade must keep a sharp edge and resist wear. Selecting a material for this is mainly driven by which factor?
questions.explain: Functionality means the material must perform its job, so a hard, wear-resistant steel is chosen for the blade.

questions.q: A designer is choosing a material for an outdoor garden bench. Which selection consideration is most critical?
questions.explain: An outdoor product must withstand rain, sun and temperature change, so durability and weather resistance are key.

questions.q: Why is cost an important factor when selecting materials for a mass-produced product?
options: It affects the final selling price and profit
questions.explain: Material cost directly influences the manufacturing cost, selling price and profit margin of a product.

questions.q: Copper is chosen for electrical cables. Which property most justifies this selection?
questions.explain: Copper is selected for wiring because it is an excellent electrical conductor as well as being ductile.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the '6 Rs' of sustainable design?
questions.explain: The 6 Rs are Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink and Repair, guiding more sustainable design decisions.

questions.q: What does 'recycle' mean in the context of sustainability?
options: Reprocessing waste material into new products
Using a product again for the same purpose
Repairing a product to extend its life
questions.explain: Recycling reprocesses used materials into new products, reducing waste and demand for raw materials.

questions.q: A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates a product's environmental impact over what period?
options: From raw material extraction to disposal
Only while it is being used
Only after it is thrown away
questions.explain: An LCA assesses environmental impact across the whole life, from raw material extraction through use to disposal.

questions.q: Most polymers are manufactured from which finite (non-renewable) resource?
questions.explain: Most polymers are derived from crude oil, a finite fossil resource that will eventually run out.

questions.q: What does a product's 'carbon footprint' measure?
options: The greenhouse gas emissions linked to its life
The physical weight of the product
The number of parts in the product
The selling price of the product
questions.explain: A carbon footprint measures the total greenhouse gas emissions, expressed as CO2, associated with a product.

questions.q: A company redesigns its packaging to use less plastic per item. Which of the 6 Rs does this best demonstrate?
questions.explain: Using less material for the same function is an example of 'Reduce', lowering resource use and waste.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Design & Technology (J310) specification; Material Considerations
